result:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two or more processes touching the same resource, so it works most of the time and occasionally corrupts or loses data.

For a log file, write each entry with a single `>>` append of one complete line:

```sh
printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg" >> "$LOG"
```

`>>` opens the file with `O_APPEND`, so the kernel moves to end-of-file and writes in one atomic step; on a local filesystem, lines from concurrent writers will not overwrite or interleave within each other. Never use `>`, and never read-modify-write the log (for example, copy to a temp file, edit, `mv` back), because another writer's lines are lost in the gap.

If an entry spans several commands or lines that must stay together, hold a lock around them:

```sh
(
  flock 9
  { echo "begin $$"; run_job; echo "end $$"; } >> "$LOG"
) 9>"$LOG.lock"
```

`flock` is advisory, so it only protects you if every writer takes the same lock file. On NFS, `O_APPEND` is not atomic across clients, so use `flock` there even for single lines, or send entries to `logger`/syslog instead.
